data.falsifier: a 2-agent crossed widening yields no cycle, or a chain yields one
data.probe_output: 7 passed (ring of 2, ring of 3, chain none, self-wait, release resolves, doctor text/json, knob off)
data.question: Does the wait-for graph over lease.waiting records expose crossed-glob deadlocks as agent cycles?

evidence.note: r-lock-cycle-selfheal (3) DETECT followed; r-everything-configurable: loops.wait_cycle, loops.wait_cycle_shown with upgrade fragments

chunk_findings.detail: When `[loops].wait_cycle_shown` is set to `0`, `cycles[:0]` is empty but the `if len(cycles) > shown` branch still fires, so `wait_findings` returns `["3 more lease deadlock(s)"]` for three cycles instead of `[]`. The knob's own doc in `ddflow/config_sections/loops.py` states "0 prints none", i.e. a user who sets 0 to silence the deadlock report still gets a `doctor` problem line emitted (and, with `on_detect = "block"`, that line can still fail the doctor), so the documented "off" position of the count knob cannot actually be reached.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/reporting/waitcycles.py:26-30 (`wait_findings`)

chunk_findings.detail: `_cycle` must tell the victim which of *its* leases to trim, but it identifies that lease as "the first lease held by `victim.agent` whose globs overlap `asked`" instead of the specific lease that actually forms the cycle edge, which is exactly `links[vi-1].blocker` (the item the predecessor is blocked on). `_remedy` then emits `ddflow update <that lease's item> --globs <keep>` and `victim_item` is set from the same lease. Given `leases = [Held("beta","V",("src/utils/**",)), Held("alpha","V",("src/**",))]` and a predecessor `P` that waits on item `alpha` with globs `("src/utils/x.py",)`, `_contested` is truthy for both of V's leases, so `next(...)` returns `beta` (first in list order). The printed remedy becomes `ddflow update beta --globs ...` (and `victim_item == "beta"`), while P is blocked on `alpha`; dropping `beta`'s globs frees nothing P needs and the deadlock persists. The lease to release is always the one named by `links[vi-1].blocker`, which the code already has and discards.

chunk_findings.detail: The item named in the "for the others" command is the *victim's own wait target* (`victim.item` in the keep branch, `victim.blocker` in the no-hold branch), not the lease the victim holds and the others are blocked on (`links[vi-1].blocker` / `links[vi-1].item`). Take a two-cycle: `P` waits on item `alpha` held by `V`, and `V` waits on item `pdoc` held by `P`. `links = [Link(agent=P,item=alpha,...), Link(agent=V,item=pdoc,...)]`; with `V` as victim, `others == ["alpha"]` and the remedy tail prints `; alpha then \`ddflow wait --item pdoc\``. `pdoc` is the item `V` is waiting for and is held by `P` itself, so the printed instruction tells `P` to wait on an item it already holds; the correct item to re-wait on is `alpha`. This mis-naming occurs on any cycle whose members wait on different items, i.e. every real instance of the deadlock this change targets.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/core/leasewait.py:_remedy

chunk_findings.detail:
The knob description rendered into `ddflow config` help says doctor names "the globs **the latest waiter** should drop", but the change's own design (EXTENDED 2026-10-15) specifies the victim is "the waiter with the **least progress**, then the latest claim". These select different agents. Concrete input: a 3-agent cycle where A has held long and completed most work, B has barely progressed, and C is the most recent claimant (say C just re-issued `ddflow wait --item`). The design's rule picks B and issues `ddflow update B --globs <without contested>`, but the help text tells the operator the victim is C ("the latest waiter"). Because the whole point is to name *the smallest release that breaks the cycle*, an operator following the help can be told to make the highest-progress (the latest-claiming) agent drop the contested globs, defeating the "least progress yields" intent. Either the emitted description must state the least-progress rule, or the algorithm must actually match "latest waiter"; as shipped the output and the documented rule disagree.

No other defect is demonstrable from this slice (the added JSON key is additive, both knobs are documented, and `wait_cycle`/`wait_cycle_shown` defaults are consistent between the templates and the snapshot).
chunk_findings.title: tests/golden/__snapshots__/test_golden_outputs.ambr:1372

chunk_findings.detail: The new expected `config --explain` block this diff records for `loops.wait_cycle` says doctor names “the globs **the latest waiter** should drop”, but the design this change is supposed to implement picks the victim as “the waiter with the **least progress**, then the latest claim” — the latest claim is only the tie-break, not the selection rule. Given the very deadlock in the intent (fleet-metrics holds the golden snapshot, fleet-logscmd waited longest with the least progress, fleet-logscale/another agent claimed the contested item most recently), the change’s own rule asks the least-progress waiter to yield, while the shipped text an operator reads tells them the most recent claimant is the one to release. A coordinator following the transcript’s documented behaviour would run `ddflow update <latest claimer> --globs <...>` against the wrong item, the contested lease is not released, and the cycle persists — exactly the 45-minute stall this change exists to break. The same block also names only `doctor` as the surface that shows the report, while the sibling `loops.*` knobs in this very file (`loops.max_repeated_failures`) enumerate every surface and the design has `status`/`brief` carry the yield request, so the golden text understates and misstates the remedy the feature prints.
